rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec hike ~90% 25bp / ~10% 50bp (CME FedWatch via Hercules); ECB Dec ~90%; BoE Dec ~80%; BoJ Dec ~84%; BoC Dec ~44%; RBA 4.85%
rows.read: A December Fed hike is still treated as all but certain, and soft US data this morning did not change that. The European Central Bank and Bank of England are also expected to hike, while Australian job losses make another Reserve Bank of Australia hike unlikely. US rates still look set to rise fastest, which keeps favouring the dollar.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: US initial claims 203K (fcst 198K), continuing 1.763M (+70K); Philly Fed 6.3 (fcst 20.6, Oct 20.9), new orders −0.4; Australia jobs Oct −43.5K, unemployment 4.9%
rows.read: US jobless claims rose a little and a Philadelphia-area factory survey fell sharply, early signs that US growth is cooling. Australia lost jobs for a second month. The US still looks firmer than most, but a run of soft figures would chip at the dollar's lead.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: Philly Fed prices paid 58.2 (Oct 43.2); UK CPI Oct 3.6%; euro-area CPI Oct 4.0%
rows.read: Inflation is still well above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. Prices paid by US factories jumped this month, a reminder that war-driven costs are still feeding through. That makes the Fed slow to read soft growth figures as a reason to stop.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: Anthropic share sale priced at $83, value above $1T; DXY ~103.70 (−0.10%); NZD/USD +0.69%
rows.read: US stock futures rose as the AI company Anthropic priced a share sale above $1 trillion. Gulf attacks continued but markets took them in stride. The dollar eased a touch, and the kiwi led a small bounce in the currencies that had fallen most.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: CFTC report of Nov 10 (out late after Veterans Day): hedge funds for USD, GBP, AUD and gold; against EUR, NZD, CAD and CHF; slightly against JPY; real money disagrees on EUR, GBP and AUD
rows.read: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds leaning toward the dollar and the pound and against the euro, the kiwi and the Canadian dollar, with bets against the kiwi growing fastest. Big long-term investors take the other side on the euro, pound and Aussie. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: ECB FSR: France debt 119% of GDP, deficit 5.5%; US October deficit $404B, a record for the month; US 10-year ~5.07%
rows.read: France's debts, flagged by the European Central Bank as a risk, keep weighing on the euro. Record US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs near 5%, which weighs a little on trust in the dollar.
